description: Reusable .NET 10 package that wraps ASP.NET Core Identity with cookie and JWT auth, Google OAuth, a pluggable e-mail provider, a multi-tenant model with dynamic RBAC (roles + module permissions), and secure defaults — wired up with a single AddMyIdentity call. JWT and Google OAuth secrets are supplied by the consumer (never shipped in the package).
releaseNotes: v4.1.0: mostly additive, with one existing-path behaviour change. Two new OVERLOADS on IMyIdentityRoleService, a new READ on IMyIdentityPermissionAdminService that names who a permission-matrix save takes access away from, and two xmldoc sentences that settle questions a consumer could not answer by reading. ExistsAsync(tenantId, displayName, excludeRoleId, ct) answers the uniqueness question a RENAME has to ask -- the two-argument overload cannot, because the role being renamed matches itself, so an unchanged name always reported as taken; the comparison is the store's normalized name, which the doc now states. GetTenantRolesAsync(tenantId, includeGlobalRoles, ct) returns the system/global roles alongside the tenant's own, so a role administration screen no longer has to query the role table to show them: visibility only, since every mutator still refuses a global role. DeleteAsync now documents that deleting a role cascades away its whole permission matrix (MyIdentityRolePermission.RoleId is a required FK), so manual cleanup before the call is redundant -- and that the cascade does NOT invoke OnBeforePermissionsRemovedAsync. SaveRolePermissionsAsync now documents that an entry at None writes no row and a module omitted from the dictionary loses its rows: unticking and omitting are the same instruction. GetUsersAffectedByPermissionChangeAsync(roleId, permissions, ct) on IMyIdentityPermissionAdminService names the users a matrix save would take permissions away from, so a consumer can WARN instead of block: until now the only tool for that moment was the OnBeforePermissionsRemovedAsync hook, which blocks and which never sees a level downgrade (Modify to Read keeps the row). All three ways of removing a permission count -- None, omitted, and lowered -- and the read validates and gates like the save it previews, sharing the same code, though its own argument checks (a null-or-whitespace roleId, a null permissions) run first and are stricter than the save's. "Affected" is scoped to the role, like GetUsersAffectedByRoleAsync: it does not subtract what a user still holds through their other roles. PERM-1: UpdateAsync's own-role exclusion during a rename is now decided by the store, by Id, in the same query that already resolves the collision, instead of a C# StringComparison.Ordinal comparison against the role's own stored NormalizedName; a rename that 4.0.0 rejected as colliding with itself may now succeed under a database collation wider than ordinal (most non-binary SQL Server collations), because that C# comparison was stricter than the collation the store enforces everywhere else. They are overloads rather than optional parameters because adding a parameter to an interface method breaks implementers and mocks; if you implement IMyIdentityRoleService or IMyIdentityPermissionAdminService yourself, there are three new members to implement across the two interfaces (the two overloads on IMyIdentityRoleService, plus GetUsersAffectedByPermissionChangeAsync on IMyIdentityPermissionAdminService). Callers upgrade with no change, unless their database collation is wider than ordinal and they rely on UpdateAsync's PERM-1 rename guard (above). Read UPGRADE.md section 36. Everything else is as 4.0.0 left it: that release was the FIRST STABLE one of the 4.x line and set the API baseline, so the surface added here is additive precisely because a breaking change to the shipped surface would now cost a major version. Consumers coming from 3.x: the v3.x -> v4.0 migration is UNCHANGED and still lives in UPGRADE.md sections 1-4 (breaking-change overview, EF Core schema migration, the per-tenant role model, and the code changes to make), with sections 5-6 as the pre-production checklist. Sections 7-36 are the per-release changelog and are historical: you do not walk them one by one, you migrate from 3.x to this release once. Dependencies are unchanged at 10.0.11 (Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Google, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer, Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.EntityFrameworkCore, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer); the ASP.NET Core shared framework is consumed through a frameworkReference, so Identity core, Blazor Components(.Authorization), Data Protection and the configuration binders are not package dependencies. Stable does NOT mean feature-complete, and the scope limits are the same ones TECHNICAL_OVERVIEW.md section 11 states: two-factor authentication is not shipped (the login status carries a forward-compatible RequiresTwoFactor signal, but there is no enrollment or verification surface); tenant isolation is enforced by the SERVICE LAYER and not by a global query filter, so ad-hoc queries you write outside the services are yours to scope; SaveRolePermissionsAsync and UpsertRolePermissionAsync are last-writer-wins on the same cell, with no typed conflict detection; and security events go to ILogger only, with no persistence seam for non-repudiation. Each of those is a deliberate boundary, documented where it bites, not an omission discovered late.
